days.name: Problem, design and foundation
days.goal: Understand the problem before any code: discovery, design, data, API, security and quality basics, then a first model call on a provider switch you can flip between Azure and local.
days.learn: What an FDE does and the mindset shift. How to ask discovery questions. Architecture, API and data-model thinking. Security basics (secrets, input validation, least privilege). Tokens, context windows and cost.

watch.title: What Is a Forward-Deployed Engineer?
This Is How Forward Deployed Engineering Is Actually Done
[1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models
watch.note: Long; watch at 1.5x or split across the evening.

read.title: Develop .NET apps with AI features (overview, with a reading order)
read.note: Open the study notes below first: they list the exact pages to read.

read.title: Generative AI for Beginners (.NET) course
read.note: Side reference all fortnight. The study notes below show which lesson folder matches which day.

days.trackA: Create or request the Azure OpenAI resource: one chat deployment, one embedding deployment, a Key Vault. Store the key in user-secrets for now.
days.trackB: Install Ollama, then pull one small chat model (phi3 or llama3.2) and nomic-embed-text. Confirm with a one-line curl or the OllamaSharp quickstart. No account needed.
build: Design pack (about 2.5 h): half-page problem statement for the IoT OpsCopilot, 10 discovery questions you would ask the operations team, architecture sketch, API list (/triage, /ask, /agent/run), data model, a 5-item threat list, and ADR 1: why this provider and model.
Project skeleton (AI allowed): solution, DI, config with a Provider setting (Azure or Ollama), logging.
By hand: an ILlmClient wrapper over IChatClient, timeouts and retry, one chat call, token and cost logged per call.
Baseline self-assessment against the 10 outline skills (1 to 5). Keep it; you repeat it on Day 10.
drills: Answer your own 10 discovery questions as if you were the customer. Where did you have to guess?
Tokenize 3 texts (short, long, code). Compare token counts and price per 1,000 calls.
Break it on purpose: wrong key, offline, 1-second timeout. Read each error and handle it.
Blank-page drill: delete your wrapper and rewrite it from memory in 15 minutes.
done: One chat call prints the answer, tokens and cost on at least one provider.
Design pack and baseline assessment saved.
Unit test: wrapper retries on a simulated 429 or timeout.
days.cut: Second-provider run; ADR 1 can be three lines.

days.name: LLM engineering: prompts and structured output
days.goal: A working feature that turns messy alert text into typed, validated JSON, and a measured comparison of two models.
days.learn: System, user and assistant roles. Few-shot examples. JSON-schema structured output. Temperature. Model selection: cost, latency, context window. Open-source and self-hosted models.

watch.title: Structured AI Output in .NET (Agent Framework + OpenAI)
One Interface for Every LLM - Microsoft.Extensions.AI
Build a .NET App that Talks to Local AI for FREE
Run AI Models Locally with Ollama (Part 1)
Let's build the GPT Tokenizer

read.title: Ollama: structured outputs
read.note: Track B. Examples are Python and JavaScript; the same format parameter exists in Ollama's API, so check how your C# client exposes it.

read.title: Chat with a local model in .NET

days.trackA: Use ChatResponseFormat with a JSON schema on the Azure OpenAI deployment. Strict schema, no retries needed in most cases.
days.trackB: Pass a JSON schema as Ollama's format parameter. Small models break the schema more often, so add a validate-and-retry loop (max 2 retries) and count how often it fires.
build: POST /triage: alert text in, typed object out (severity, probable cause, next step, confidence).
Write your own system prompt and 3 few-shot examples. Keep prompts in files, not strings in code.
Run the same 10 sample alerts through two models (or Azure plus local). Fill a table: valid JSON rate, correct severity, latency, tokens, cost.
Fake-model xUnit test: the endpoint handles valid, invalid and empty model replies.
drills: Write 3 prompt variants and score each on the same 10 alerts. Keep the winner and note why.
Feed an ambiguous alert and a nonsense alert. What does the model do? Add handling.
Change temperature from 0 to 1. Run each 5 times. Is the output stable?
Stuff a long text until you hit the context window. Record the error and the cost.
Blank-page drill: rewrite the schema and the validator from memory.
done: Swagger returns valid typed JSON for 10 of 10 samples on at least one model.
Comparison table filled with real numbers.
Fake-model tests green.
days.cut: The second-model live run (keep the code path and note it as not run).

days.name: Tool calling over real data
days.goal: The model can ask your code for data. You write the tools and control exactly what they may do.
days.learn: Tool schema, the call and result round trip, argument validation, read-only versus write tools, parameterised SQL. Why a model must never run raw SQL.

watch.title: C# - OpenAI API Function Calling Tutorial
Function Calling in Azure OpenAI Service
Advanced Tool Calling in Microsoft Agent Framework
watch.note: Optional: uses a framework; you hand-write yours.

read.title: Tool use overview (Claude)
read.note: Good diagram of the request and result loop.

read.title: SQLite quick start (plus the two other pages you need)
read.note: Track B database. The study notes below list the three pages worth reading.

days.trackA: Telemetry in Azure SQL (Readings, Alerts, Devices). Connect with managed identity later; a connection string in user-secrets is fine today.
days.trackB: Same tables in a SQLite file. Keep the schema identical so only the connection changes. Check the model's page on ollama.com for a tools tag before relying on tool calling.
build: Telemetry generator (AI allowed): 50 devices, 24 hours, a minute apart, with a few planted faults.
By hand, 3 read-only tools: GetRecentReadings(deviceId, minutes), GetAlerts(deviceId, since), GetDeviceStatus(deviceId). Parameterised queries only.
By hand: one tool-calling round: send tool schemas, run the requested tool, return the result, get the final answer.
Validate every argument (type, range, known device) before touching the database.
drills: Ask something that needs no tool. The model should not call one.
Ask about device 999. Return a clean error the model can explain.
Pass an argument like ' OR 1=1 --. Prove it is harmless.
Ask a question that needs two tools. What does your single round miss? (You fix it on Day 6.)
Blank-page drill: rewrite one tool and its schema from memory.
done: 'Which devices exceeded temperature in the last hour?' is answered correctly from the database.
Tool functions have tests that need no model.
5 tool questions added to the golden set.

days.name: Embeddings, chunking and the vector store
days.goal: Turn your runbooks into searchable vectors and see for yourself how chunking changes what is found.
days.learn: Embeddings and cosine similarity. Chunk size and overlap. Metadata. Semantic versus keyword search. What a vector store keeps.

watch.title: Embeddings and Vector Databases for RAG: Semantic Search Explained
RAG #2: Chunking, Embeddings and Vector Databases Explained
Chunking in RAG (hands-on in LangChain and LlamaIndex)

read.title: Build a vector search app (quickstart)
read.note: In-memory store; works in both tracks.

days.trackA: Embeddings from your Azure embedding deployment. Optionally index in Azure AI Search later; the in-memory store is enough today.
days.trackB: Embeddings from nomic-embed-text on Ollama. In-memory vector store saved to a JSON or SQLite file so you do not re-embed every run.
build: Small dataset: 20 runbooks of about 300 words each (5 device types by 4 failure modes). Write 8 yourself, generate the rest with AI, then edit them. Put the file name and title in each.
By hand: a chunker with size and overlap settings (and optionally heading-aware splitting).
By hand: the ingest pipeline: read, chunk, embed, store with metadata (file, chunk number).
A search command that prints the top 5 chunks with score and source.
drills: Try 3 chunk sizes on 10 queries. Which wins, and why?
Search with a typo, a synonym and a question in different words.
Search for something that is not in any runbook. How low are the scores?
Estimate the embedding cost of 10,000 documents.
Blank-page drill: rewrite the chunker from memory, with a test for the edge cases.
done: Top 5 results look sensible for 10 queries.
Chunker tests cover empty input, overlap and the final chunk.
Ingest can be rerun without duplicates.
days.cut: Azure AI Search and pgvector. Stay on the in-memory store.

days.name: RAG with citations and retrieval evaluation
days.goal: A document assistant that answers from your runbooks, cites its sources, says 'I do not know' when it should, and is measured.
days.learn: Grounding prompts, citations, refusal, prompt injection hidden in documents, hit rate and MRR, RAG versus fine-tuning versus prompt engineering.

watch.title: RAG C# Application with Microsoft.Extensions.AI, Ollama and Qdrant
watch.note: C#. Uses Qdrant; you keep the in-memory store.

watch.title: Build a fully local AI RAG app - as simple as possible!
RAG Evaluation: Measuring Retrieval, Grounding and Drift

read.title: Azure AI Search: retrieval-augmented generation overview
Hugging Face: LoRA chapter (for the RAG vs fine-tuning section)
read.note: Skim the 'when to fine-tune' reasoning only.

days.trackA: Chat deployment answers from retrieved chunks. Same prompt as Track B.
days.trackB: A local model answers from retrieved chunks. Expect weaker answers and more refusals; record the difference, it is part of the learning.
build: POST /ask: embed the question, retrieve top k, build the grounded prompt, return the answer with citations like [file#chunk].
Refuse when the best score is under a threshold, with a clear message.
Golden set of 25 questions: 20 answerable (with expected source file) and 5 unanswerable.
By hand: an eval runner that prints hit at 3, MRR and refusal accuracy.
Plant one malicious sentence in a runbook ('ignore previous instructions...'). Record whether the model obeys it, then harden the prompt.
drills: Tune k and the threshold. Record the effect on hit at 3 and refusal accuracy.
Run the same 25 questions with no retrieval at all. How much does RAG add?
Read 5 wrong answers and label each: retrieval failure or generation failure.
Write down in 5 lines when you would pick fine-tuning, RAG or prompting for this project.
Blank-page drill: rewrite the grounded prompt builder from memory.
done: Eval table printed: hit at 3, MRR, refusal accuracy, with and without retrieval.
Test proves every citation points to a chunk that was actually retrieved.
Injection test result written down.

days.name: Agent loop with human approval
days.goal: A multi-step agent that uses your tools and your RAG, stops at a safe limit, and cannot take a write action without your approval.
days.learn: Agent loop (decide, act, observe, repeat). Step limits and state. Retrieval as a tool. Human-in-the-loop. Audit trail. When a fixed workflow beats an agent.

watch.title: Build Your First AI Agent in C# (Microsoft Agent Framework, Ep. 1)
watch.note: Concepts; you hand-write the loop first.

watch.title: .NET AI Community Standup: Getting Started with the Microsoft Agent Framework
Build Your First AI Agent in C# with Microsoft Agent Framework (.NET 10)

read.title: Generative AI for Beginners (.NET): lesson 4, agents

days.trackA: Chat model on Azure OpenAI drives the loop.
days.trackB: Local model drives the loop. If it cannot call tools reliably, use the local model for answers and a hosted API key for the loop only for this day, or script the model with a fake for the tests.
build: By hand, no framework: loop of messages, model reply, tool calls, execute, append results, repeat until a final answer or 8 steps.
Tools: your 3 telemetry tools plus search_runbooks (your Day 5 RAG).
Two write actions: AcknowledgeAlert and CreateTicket. Each pauses and asks for approval (console prompt or a pending-approval endpoint).
Audit log table: every step, tool, arguments, result, approver.
drills: Ask an impossible request. The agent should stop or ask, not loop.
Use a fake model that never finishes. Prove the step limit stops it.
Deny an approval. The agent must adapt, not retry forever.
Compare the agent to a fixed 3-step workflow on 5 questions. Which is better and why?
Blank-page drill: rewrite the loop skeleton from memory.
done: 'Device 7 is overheating: diagnose and acknowledge the alert' runs end to end and pauses for approval.
Tests with a fake model: step limit, approve path, deny path.
Audit log shows each step.

days.name: MCP server and client
days.goal: Move your tools behind a Model Context Protocol server so any MCP-aware client can use them, and make your agent a client of it.
days.learn: MCP architecture, tools versus resources and prompts, stdio versus HTTP transport, least privilege for exposed tools.

watch.title: Build an MCP server with .NET 10
C# MCP server and client with GitHub Models
watch.note: Uses GitHub Models for the client; Track B swaps in your Ollama chat client.

watch.title: Build an MCP Server in ASP.NET Core From Scratch

read.title: Build Your First MCP Server in C# (blog)
What is MCP? (introduction, with the three pages to read)

days.trackA: Server and client are the same code in both tracks; only the chat client registration differs.
days.trackB: Same code. The MCP part needs no cloud at all, so this day is identical.
build: New MCP server project exposing your 3 telemetry tools and search_runbooks. Write the tool code by hand.
Gate the write actions: expose them only when a setting is on, and keep approval on the agent side.
Replace the agent's in-process tools with an MCP client that lists and calls the server's tools over stdio.
Snapshot test of the server's tool list.
drills: Connect a second MCP client or an inspector tool to your server and list the tools.
Add a new tool to the server. The agent should see it with no agent code change.
Call a tool with bad arguments over MCP. Check the error.
Remove the write tools from the server. Does the agent adapt?
Blank-page drill: write a new one-tool MCP server from memory.
done: The golden tool and agent questions give the same answers through MCP as on Day 6.
Server tool-list snapshot test green.
Draw the final architecture so far (stack diagram).
days.cut: HTTP transport and the optional second client.

days.name: Evaluation, guardrails and CI
days.goal: Prove it works and make it safer: measure quality and hallucination, block the obvious attacks, and run it all in CI.
days.learn: Hallucination types, groundedness, LLM-as-judge and its limits, input and output guardrails, tool permissions, OWASP LLM risks (prompt injection, excessive agency, sensitive data), evaluation in CI.

watch.title: LLM as a Judge: Evaluating AI with AI for Hallucination Detection
DeepEval Tutorial Part 2: Answer Relevancy, Faithfulness and Hallucination Detection
watch.note: Python library; take the metric ideas, write your own in C#.

days.trackA: Judge model: your Azure chat deployment, ideally a larger one than the answering model.
days.trackB: Judge model: local model, which is weaker. Add rule-based checks (must contain a citation, cited file exists, answer length) and compare the judge with your own labels.
build: Input guardrails: length limit, simple injection patterns, PII masking.
Output guardrails: must cite or refuse, schema valid, no tool names leaked.
Tool permission policy: allow-list, step limit, rate limit, write actions need approval.
By hand: LLM-as-judge groundedness score (1 to 5) plus the rule checks.
Grow the golden set to about 40: add tool, approval and 8 attack cases.
GitHub Actions: build, unit tests, and an eval on recorded or fake model replies (no live calls in CI).
drills: Write 5 attacks: in the user message, in a runbook, in a tool argument. Record which are blocked.
Label 10 answers yourself, then compare with the judge. Where does it disagree?
Change the prompt on purpose to make it worse. Does the eval catch it?
Blank-page drill: write the golden-set loader and metric calculation from memory.
done: CI is green.
One-page evaluation report: hit at 3, MRR, refusal accuracy, groundedness, attack block rate, before and after.
Every guardrail has a test.
days.cut: Judge model: use only the rule checks and say so in the report.

days.name: AI-assisted delivery, deployment and monitoring
days.goal: Use an AI coding assistant the way the outline asks (to ship a feature with tests, review and security), then deploy and monitor the whole thing.
days.learn: Spec-driven work with a coding agent, reviewing generated code, security review checklist. Containers, secrets and managed identity, logs, traces, tokens and cost.

How the GitHub Copilot coding agent works (Checkout)

days.trackA: Deploy API and MCP server to App Service or Container Apps with managed identity, secrets from Key Vault, telemetry to Application Insights.
days.trackB: docker compose up on your machine. Secrets from environment variables. OpenTelemetry console or file exporter, plus a small script that reports latency, tokens and cost per request.
build: Feature by AI: write a short spec for POST /incident-report (summarise an incident from the audit log). Let your coding assistant implement it.

By hand: read the diff line by line, write 3 tests yourself, run the security checklist (secrets, input validation, PII in logs, excessive agency). Write a review note listing what the AI got wrong or missed.
Dockerfile and compose file (AI allowed for boilerplate).
Deploy (Track A) or compose up (Track B). Log every model call with tokens, latency and cost.
drills: Stop the model endpoint. The app must fail gracefully and log it.
Estimate cost per 100 requests from your own logs.
Rotate a secret and redeploy without code changes.
Blank-page drill: write the model-call logging middleware from memory.
done: A running container (cloud URL or localhost) answers a question end to end.
Logs show per-call tokens, latency and cost.
The AI-review note exists and names at least 3 real findings.
days.cut: Cloud deployment. A working local compose setup counts.

days.name: Fine-tuning experiment, capstone package and final review
days.goal: Experiment with fine-tuning, finish the capstone package, and prove progress against the outline.
days.learn: LoRA and QLoRA, datasets, training versus inference cost, and what training from scratch involves (concept only). Final presentation structure.

watch.title: LoRA and QLoRA Fine-tuning Explained In-Depth
LoRA and QLoRA Explained Simply
Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out
watch.note: Concept only: watch selectively for how training from scratch works.

days.trackA: Experiment on a free notebook GPU if you can get one (Google Colab needs a Google account; free GPU availability is not guaranteed and was not verified).
days.trackB: No GPU: use a very small open model on CPU with about 100 examples, only to see the pipeline and compare with your prompted triage. If that is impossible, write a one-page decision memo: fine-tune, RAG or prompt for this project, with cost estimates.
build: Fine-tuning experiment (2 h timebox): turn about 100 of your Day 2 alerts and answers into a small dataset, run a LoRA fine-tune of a small open model, compare against your prompted version on 10 held-out alerts. A poor result is fine; write down why.
Capstone package: README, final architecture diagram, ADRs, evaluation report, setup steps for both tracks.
10-minute demo script and a half-page non-technical stakeholder update.
Repeat the baseline self-assessment from Day 1 and compare.
drills: Present the demo aloud to a colleague or a recording.
Answer these cold: why this chunk size, why an approval gate, what MCP added, how you would reduce cost by half.
List what you would do with 3 more weeks.
done: Demo runs end to end.
Docs and evaluation report complete.
Final self-assessment filled; fine-tuning result or decision memo written.
